title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
formal: Do there exist real constants \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge1\), some stabilizer code on \(n\ge N\) qubits has an admissible list of checks as defined below and satisfies \[k\ge rn,\qquad d\ge\delta n,\qquad H\succeq\frac{s}{n}D_Q?\] Here \(k\) is its number of logical qubits, \(d\) its code distance, each listed check acts on at most \(w\) qubits, and each qubit occurs in at most \(b\) listed checks. All five constants are fixed for the unbounded family. This is the bounded-degree stabilizer version of asymptotically good quantum local testability.
definitions:
The physical Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). In the standard one-qubit basis, \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). The Pauli group consists of tensor products of \(I,X,Y,Z\), multiplied by phases from \(\{1,-1,i,-i\}\). A Pauli's support is the set of positions with a nonidentity tensor factor, and its weight is the cardinality of that set; the scalar phase does not affect support.

An admissible stabilizer presentation is a finite nonempty list \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) of Hermitian Pauli checks of positive weight. Hermitian means \(S_j=S_j^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose. The checks commute pairwise, and the group they generate does not contain \(-I\). Its code space is \[Q=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_n:S_j\psi=\psi\text{ for every }j\}.\] This nonzero space has dimension \(2^k\); the target requires \(k\ge1\). The distance \(d\) is the minimum weight of a Pauli \(P\) that preserves \(Q\), meaning \(P(Q)=Q\), but whose restriction to \(Q\) is not a scalar multiple of identity. For a stabilizer code with \(k\ge1\), such logical Paulis exist. This distance concerns undetectable changes to encoded information. The rate is \(k/n\) and the relative distance is \(d/n\).

The checks need not be independent, and a list may contain repetitions. The bounds refer to that actual list: \(\operatorname{wt}(S_j)\le w\) for every \(j\), and each qubit belongs to the supports of at most \(b\) checks, counting repetitions separately. Both are maximum bounds, not average bounds. Define the normalized check Hamiltonian \[H=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{I-S_j}{2}.\] Each summand is the orthogonal projection onto the failing eigenspace of one check. If a check is selected uniformly, the rejection probability on a unit vector \(\phi\) is \(\langle\phi,H\phi\rangle\); on a density matrix \(\rho\) it is \(\operatorname{Tr}(H\rho)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one.

For \(0\le t\le n\), let \(Q_t\) be the complex linear span of vectors \(E\psi\), where \(\psi\in Q\) and \(E\) ranges over Pauli errors of weight at most \(t\). Let \(\Pi_t\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(Q_t\). These spaces are nested, with \(Q_0=Q\) and \(Q_n=\mathcal H_n\). Define \[D_Q=\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(I-\Pi_t)=\sum_{t=1}^n t(\Pi_t-\Pi_{t-1}).\] The two expressions agree by telescoping. The eigenvalue \(t\) measures the error radius of the corresponding orthogonal layer. Using Pauli errors in the span is equivalent to using arbitrary operators supported on at most \(t\) qubits, since local Pauli products span all such operators. This is not trace distance between density matrices.

The inequality \(H\succeq(s/n)D_Q\) means its difference is positive semidefinite: \(\langle\phi,[H-(s/n)D_Q]\phi\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(\phi\in\mathcal H_n\), where \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Equivalently it holds in expectation for every density matrix. The number \(s\) is normalized soundness. The family may use an arbitrary unbounded sequence of lengths rather than every integer length. Checks may connect any qubits, without geometric locality. No CSS restriction, efficient construction, decoding algorithm or transversal-gate property is required.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that fixed constants and an unbounded family satisfying all conditions exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\), there is a finite length bound beyond which no admissible presentation satisfies all the conditions simultaneously. An existence proof need not provide a polynomial-time construction. A failure for one proposed family, one subclass such as CSS codes, or one geometry does not prove nonexistence. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance, a growing maximum check weight or incidence, and a soundness guarantee confined to selected error weights do not meet the target. The operator inequality must cover the entire physical Hilbert space. This is an exact existence question, not a numerical approximation task.
why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.

importance.reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.

status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the full primary distance-operator definition and parameter results, corrected Dinur–Lin–Vidick v3 and Li–Li–Liu v2 statements and revision histories, primary tensor-product abstract and a bounded later-work search were checked. No family simultaneously meeting constant rate, relative distance, maximum check weight, maximum incidence and normalized soundness was identified. Existing inverse-polylogarithmic losses and growing-locality results do not meet this target. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

The distance operator measures distance from the entire code space, not the written weight of one chosen Pauli error. A stabilizer leaves every codeword unchanged, while a logical Pauli can change the encoded information and still stay inside the code space. Both therefore remain at distance zero from the code as a subspace. The nested spaces \(Q_t\) account for these identifications. The operator inequality also controls superpositions and mixed states, not only individual Pauli-corrupted codewords.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has \(k=\Omega (n)\), distance \(\Omega (n/\log ^{3}n)\), soundness \(\Omega (1/\log ^{3}n)\), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.

Garg and Sengupta obtain a further constant-soundness result using algebraic-geometry codes. Their stated application has locality growing as the square root of code length. This still misses the maximum constant check weight required here.

sentences: A locally testable quantum code should reveal a substantial error by checking only a few qubits.
The desired family must also encode a linear amount of quantum information and tolerate errors on a linear number of physical qubits.
Each check and each qubit's participation in checks must remain bounded as the code grows.
These requirements strengthen ordinary good quantum LDPC codes by demanding a quantitative relation between distance from the code space and rejection probability.
Such codes would connect robust quantum error detection with the complexity of low-energy states and the broader search for quantum PCP constructions.
